taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Anatherum virginicum and treats Andropogon virginicus as a homotypic synonym. Retain the familiar Andropogon name as a primary search alias because most Texas field material still uses it.
look_here_first: Look for narrow silky racemes tucked partly inside flattened spathe-like upper sheaths. Mature plants often turn straw to orange-brown and hold the pale silky seedheads into winter. It does not make the dense brushy crown of bushy bluestem or the digitate turkey foot of big bluestem.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew accepts Anatherum virginicum and explicitly maps Andropogon virginicus into the accepted concept. USDA-derived county distribution under the familiar Andropogon virginicus name supports Hays, Real, and San Saba, all inside the project target zone.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Synonym-based county evidence is counted only because current Kew treatment explicitly links Andropogon virginicus to accepted Anatherum virginicum; do not infer counties from statewide or ecoregional presence.

best_field_traits: narrow silky racemes partly enclosed by spathe-like upper sheaths
silky hairs around spikelets create a pale fluffy look
mature clumps commonly turn straw to orange-brown and persist into winter
seedhead branches remain narrower and less brushlike than bushy bluestem
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Anatherum glomeratum has a much denser, broader brushlike crown. Andropogon gerardi has open digitate turkey-foot racemes and a taller prairie-grass architecture.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Broomsedge has narrow silky racemes tucked in upper sheaths; bushy bluestem forms a dense brushlike crown, while big bluestem carries a few open turkey-foot racemes.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: Broomsedge: follow a flowering culm upward and find many narrow silky racemes partly tucked into flattened leafy spathes, usually separated along the upper stem rather than packed into one bushy terminal crown. Brown winter color supports recognition but does not prove identity.
crew_checkpoints: Photograph the entire rooted clump and upper flowering stem, showing the spacing of spathe-enclosed units.
Open one mature spathe without destroying its connection to the stem; photograph paired racemes and the spathe with a millimeter scale.
Use a hand lens to document paired sessile and pedicellate spikelets, rachis hairs and awn attachment; record actual dimensions from the specimen.
Photograph the ligule and collar in focus, and compare the same structures against bushy bluestem.

look_alikes.check: Bushy bluestem produces a broad densely crowded brushlike terminal cluster of many short hairy racemes, unlike the more individually separated broomsedge spathes.
Little bluestem has silky racemes on distinct branches; compare branch arrangement, spathes and mature spikelet pairs rather than winter color.
Big bluestem usually shows a few exposed turkey-foot branches instead of numerous spathe-enclosed narrow units.

vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 Phytoneuron 2015-4 page 34, Texas Hill Country vegetative key
vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.look_here_first: Instead of winter color, inspect fresh upper sheaths: broomsedge margins usually mostly smooth, sometimes outer edge ciliate, while bushy has hairs on both inner and outer margins and more strongly compressed, keeled sheaths.
vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.photo_handoff: Confirm with a macro of each sheath MARGIN and the exact 1–2mm membranous ligule; no arrow until pixels establish which margin is pictured.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: BROOMSEDGE = more individually separated silky, spathe-held upper racemes; BUSHY = dense clustered terminal brush. A. tenuispatheum is separate accepted species, not just another photo of either.
